exp.0:12:
He says he had many more things to tell his friend, but he prefers not to write them down with ink and pen, that is, in a letter. The word "but" in the verse is the English "but" used here as a transition, so the sentence is explained here as "but." The verses that follow explain why: he hopes to visit him soon and speak with him face to face.

The one speaking is "the elder," as he introduces himself at the beginning of this letter. Tradition identifies him with John the apostle, although the letter does not give his name. He is writing to Gaius, a dear brother who helps believers who are traveling. After praising Gaius and warning him about Diotrephes, the author closes warmly and leaves the other matters for a conversation in person.

Some things are better said face to face than in writing. Today, instead of settling everything through messages, we can make a visit or a phone call to encourage someone, clear up a misunderstanding, or share what we feel from the heart.
exp.0:0:
Here the author presents himself as "the elder" and greets Gaius warmly, calling him "the wellbeloved." He says he loves him "in the truth," that is, with a sincere love, not with empty words or mere politeness. The word "whom" here means "to whom" in the sense of the person being loved.

The writer calls himself only "the elder." Tradition identifies him with the apostle John, although the letter does not give his name. Gaius was a believer known for his hospitality toward the brothers who traveled. John writes to encourage him and to clarify who truly walks in the truth.

Today we can imitate this greeting. Think of a brother or sister in your church and tell them today, sincerely, that you value them and that you pray for them. A simple and true message can strengthen another person a great deal.
exp.0:1:
John tells his dear friend Gaius that he wishes everything may go well for him and that he may be in good health, just as his soul is already doing well. "Prospered" means that things go well for him, and "in all things" means "in every way." The soul's "prospering" refers to his spiritual life, which is healthy and firm.

The one speaking is "the elder," whom many understand to be the apostle John, although the letter does not give his name. He writes to Gaius, a believer known for his faithfulness and for welcoming the brothers who traveled. This greeting was common in letters of the time, and here John joins it with a sincere wish of affection. It is not a promise of wealth, but a prayer for his well-being.

Today we can pray for the people we love, asking for health and well-being for them, but caring first for their spiritual life. May our inner peace grow more than anything else.
exp.0:4:
He says that Gaius, whom John calls "beloved," acts faithfully in everything he does for the brothers, even for those he does not know. "Faithfully" means with loyalty and steadiness. "Strangers" here refers to believers from other places who came to visit, not necessarily people of another nationality.

The speaker is John, the elder, who writes a personal letter to Gaius. The traveling believers, probably missionaries sent to preach, had been welcomed warmly by Gaius. John rejoices and encourages him to keep helping them. It is not known with certainty who this Gaius was, since several men had that name.

Today we can imitate Gaius: open the door, and give food, lodging, or help to those who serve God or are in need, even if we do not know them well. Small acts of hospitality, done faithfully, please God.
exp.0:7:
The explanation says that believers ought to welcome and support those who go out to preach the gospel. Here "welcome" includes giving them lodging and help for the journey. "Such" refers to those traveling brothers, and "fellowhelpers to the truth" means co-workers with them in God's work.

The elder John writes to his beloved friend Gaius. Some missionaries sent by John had traveled out of love for Christ, asking nothing from unbelievers. Gaius had received them well, while Diotrephes, out of pride, rejected them. John encourages Gaius to keep supporting them.

Today we can support missionaries, pastors, or brothers and sisters who serve, through prayer, offerings, lodging, or a word of encouragement. In this way we share in their work, even if we ourselves do not go out to preach.
exp.0:6:
It says that some brothers went out to preach and to serve for love of the name of Christ, and that they did not accept help from the Gentiles, that is, from those who did not believe in God. "Their name" refers to the name of Jesus. "Gentiles" here means people outside the faith.

The one speaking is John, called "the elder," who writes to his dear friend Gaius. The traveling brothers were missionaries who had been well received by Gaius. John explains that they did not ask anything from unbelievers, so that no one would think they were preaching for money. That is why believers should support them.

For today: give generously to those who serve God sincerely, whether through prayer, offerings, or hospitality. In this way you take part in their work and help the gospel move forward.
exp.0:2:
The writer felt great joy when some brothers arrived and reported on how Gaius lives out the truth. The explanation notes that the wording behind "I rejoiced greatly" is about being glad, and that the phrase rendered "testified of the truth" means they spoke well of Gaius's faith. Walking in the truth means living according to what he believes.

The one speaking is identified as the elder, traditionally understood to be the apostle John, although the letter does not give his name. He writes to Gaius, whom he loves as a friend and as a child in the faith. Some traveling believers came back with good news about Gaius's conduct, and this encouraged John greatly.

For today: our faith shows in the way we live, not only in what we say. Strive for your way of treating others, your honesty, and your service to give a good witness of Christ. Also be ready to rejoice and to encourage others when you see them doing well in their faith.
exp.0:11:
It says that everyone speaks well of Demetrius, and even "the truth itself" backs him up, meaning that his life agrees with what the gospel teaches. John and those who are with him also give a good testimony. "Ye know" means "you know." John reminds them that his word can be trusted.

The one speaking is John, the elder, and he writes to Gaius, a beloved brother. Diotrephes refused to receive the brothers who traveled teaching. For this reason John presents Demetrius, probably the one carrying the letter, so that they will receive him well. Some believe he was a messenger; the text does not say this with certainty.

For today: value and support people whose lives confirm what they say they believe. Also seek to have your own character speak well of Christ. Before following anyone, look at their conduct and at what other healthy believers say about them.
exp.0:9:
He says that John, if he comes to visit them, will call attention to what Diotrephes is doing. This man speaks evil of John and his companions with malicious words (harmful speech full of ill intent). Besides this, he does not welcome the brothers who arrive, prevents others from receiving them, and throws out of the church those who do.

The one speaking is John, who in this letter calls himself "the elder," and he writes to his friend Gaius. There were missionaries who traveled preaching and needed lodging. Diotrephes, who wanted to be first, turned them away. John wants Gaius to keep supporting them. We do not know in detail what teaching or conflict lay behind this.

For today: examine whether the desire to have first place leads you to shut the door on others. Practice hospitality, and give generously to those who serve with humility.
exp.0:10:
This verse tells Gaius: do not imitate what is wrong; follow what is good. "Beloved" is an affectionate way of addressing him. The verse's own wording, "Beloved, follow not that which is evil, but that which is good," is the same message. Whoever does good shows that they belong to God; whoever does evil has not seen God, meaning they do not truly know him.

The elder John is speaking, in a personal letter to his friend Gaius. He tells him that Diotrephes, who wanted to be first, was speaking badly about them and was not welcoming the brothers who traveled teaching. For this reason John warns Gaius not to copy that bad example. He then mentions Demetrius as someone worthy of imitation.

Today, before following someone's example, look at how they treat others. Imitate those who serve with humility and welcome others, and avoid pride, gossip and harshness, even when they come from people in authority.
exp.0:8:
The explanation says that the author wrote a letter to the church, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first and most important among them, does not receive them. The word meaning first place and command is rewritten here as "loves to be first and most important," which matches the verse. The phrase about not accepting or welcoming the author's messengers is rendered as "does not receive them."

The one who speaks is the elder, as he introduces himself at the beginning of the letter, and he writes to Gaius. The traveling missionary brothers who went preaching needed lodging and support. Diotrephes rejected them, spoke badly of the author, and even expelled those who wanted to help them. We do not know exactly what his office was, but his attitude is clear.

For today: examine your heart. Serve in your church without seeking to be the center, and welcome kindly others who work for the gospel.
exp.0:3:
It says that for the author there is no greater joy than to know that his children live according to the truth. The author's own words say he has no greater joy than to hear that his children walk in truth, so the explanation here refers to news reaching him about them. "Walk" is the everyday way of describing how a person lives day by day. "Truth" refers to what God teaches and to living it out for real.

The one speaking is the elder, as he presents himself in verse 1, and Christian tradition identifies him with John. He writes to Gayo, whom he loves. When he says "my children," he is speaking with affection of people he has guided in the faith, not necessarily of children by blood. Some traveling brothers told him that Gayo was living faithfully, and that gladdened him greatly.

For today: if you guide or accompany others in the faith, rejoice when they grow and live out what they believe. Encourage them with a word or a prayer, and seek to make your own life consistent with the truth you teach.
exp.0:13:
He says that the author hopes to visit Gaius soon and talk with him "face to face," that is, in person. He wishes him "peace," a greeting that means well-being and harmony. He sends greetings from the friends who are with him and asks Gaius to greet the friends there, one by one, "by name." The words "to" and "shortly" are old forms; today we would say "to" and "soon."

The one speaking is "the elder," as he introduces himself at the beginning of the letter, and he writes to his dear Gaius. He does not say everything in writing, because he prefers to speak in person. Little is discussed about who this elder is; Christian tradition has identified him with John, although the letter does not give his name.

Today we can imitate this personal care. Some things are better said in person. Also, greeting others by name shows them that they are valued. This week, visit or call someone and acknowledge them by name.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that some traveling brothers spoke before the church about the love Gaius showed them. John asks Gaius to keep helping them on their way in a manner worthy of God, and he assures him that by doing so he will do well, meaning he will do something good and right.

John, now an elderly man, writes to his dear friend Gaius. He is glad that Gaius lives in the truth and has welcomed with hospitality the brothers who went out to preach the gospel. They did not accept help from unbelievers, so they depended on the generosity of fellow Christians. John wants Gaius to keep supporting them.

For today: think of someone who serves God, such as a missionary, a pastor, or a teacher, and help that person in a concrete way. You can pray for them, give them an offering, host them, or encourage them with a message.

sum.0: The elder writes to his beloved Gaius to commend him for walking in the truth and for faithfully supporting the brothers who travel around preaching. He asks him to keep on helping them, and he warns that Diotrephes, who loves to be first, refuses to welcome the brothers and speaks evil of them. He encourages Gaius to keep following what is good, and he speaks highly of Demetrius.
